question_text: Klumpke palsy typically results from injury to which spinal roots?
explanation_text: Klumpke palsy is a lower trunk (C8-T1) injury and may include Horner syndrome if T1 sympathetics are involved.

question_text: The thoracic duct typically drains into which venous site?
explanation_text: The thoracic duct drains lymph from most of the body into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins).

question_text: A lesion of the right optic tract produces which visual field defect?
explanation_text: Each optic tract carries contralateral visual field information, so a right tract lesion causes left homonymous hemianopia.

question_text: Which of the following is a neural crest derivative?
explanation_text: Adrenal medulla chromaffin cells arise from neural crest; adrenal cortex is mesodermal.

question_text: Which of the following is the most important determinant of myocardial oxygen demand?
explanation_text: Myocardial O2 demand is driven mainly by heart rate, contractility, and wall tension (afterload/preload via Laplace).

question_text: The Bohr effect describes which of the following?
option_a: Increased PO2 decreases CO2 binding to hemoglobin
option_b: Increased PCO2 or H+ decreases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen
option_d: Fetal hemoglobin has lower oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin
explanation_text: The Bohr effect: raised PCO2 and H+ shift the O2-Hb curve to the right, unloading oxygen in metabolically active tissues.

question_text: ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct via which receptor and channel?
explanation_text: V2 receptor activation raises cAMP, inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of principal cells.

question_text: Von Gierke disease (GSD I) is caused by deficiency of:
explanation_text: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency prevents hepatic glucose release, causing severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly.

question_text: The urea cycle takes place primarily in which organ and which cellular compartments?
explanation_text: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase are mitochondrial; later urea-cycle steps are cytosolic, mainly in hepatocytes.

question_text: Describe the blood supply of the heart. Add a note on dominance and referred pain of angina.
sample_answer_text:
Heart and coronary arteries is a high-yield KUHS theory topic. Start with a one-line definition or formation, then organised headings the examiner can tick, and finish with a clinical correlation or applied anatomy note.

Right and left coronary arteries arise from the anterior and left posterior aortic sinuses. RCA runs in the right AV groove, gives SA nodal (in ~60%), right marginal, and usually the posterior descending artery in right dominance. LCA divides into LAD (anterior IV groove, diagonals, septal perforators) and circumflex (left AV groove, obtuse marginals). Venous drainage is mainly the coronary sinus (great, middle, small cardiac veins) into the right atrium; anterior cardiac veins drain directly to RA. Most people are right-dominant (PDA from RCA). Left dominance (PDA from LCx) is less common. Ischaemic pain is referred to the left arm, jaw and epigastrium via T1–T4 sympathetics sharing dermatomes with the heart.

question_text: Describe the inguinal canal. Differentiate direct and indirect inguinal hernia.
sample_answer_text:
Inguinal canal and hernia is a high-yield KUHS theory topic. Start with a one-line definition or formation, then organised headings the examiner can tick, and finish with a clinical correlation or applied anatomy note.

The inguinal canal is an oblique 4 cm passage in the lower anterior abdominal wall, above the inguinal ligament, from deep to superficial inguinal rings. Contents: spermatic cord (or round ligament) and ilioinguinal nerve (which enters the canal rather than the deep ring). Boundaries (MALT): roof — muscles (internal oblique, transversus); anterior — aponeurosis of external oblique (and internal oblique laterally); floor — inguinal ligament and lacunar ligament; posterior — transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by conjoint tendon. Indirect hernia leaves through the deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, and may follow the processus vaginalis into the scrotum; it is often congenital. Direct hernia bulges through Hesselbach triangle, medial to inferior epigastric vessels, and is acquired from posterior-wall weakness. Coverings differ: indirect has extra peritoneal processes along the cord; both can strangulate.

question_text: Describe the femoral triangle. Add a note on the adductor (Hunter) canal.
sample_answer_text:
Femoral triangle and adductor canal is a high-yield KUHS theory topic. Start with a one-line definition or formation, then organised headings the examiner can tick, and finish with a clinical correlation or applied anatomy note.

Femoral triangle is in the upper thigh: base is inguinal ligament, lateral sartorius, medial adductor longus; floor is iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus; roof is fascia lata, cribriform fascia and skin. Contents lateral to medial (NAVY): femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-empty (femoral canal with lymph node of Cloquet). Femoral sheath encloses artery, vein and canal, not the nerve. Femoral hernia is more common in females, appears below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and has a high strangulation risk at the rigid femoral ring. Adductor canal (Hunter) runs from the apex of the triangle to the adductor hiatus, under sartorius, with vastus medialis lateral and adductors posterior. It contains femoral artery and vein, saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis; a site for adductor-canal block and for femoral-artery ligation in some trauma protocols.
